# Game design
<!-- Generated by scripts/generate_docs.py from scripts/templates/game-design.md. Edit the template. -->

Last Breath is a hold-and-spin game with no base game. A bet buys one dive, which is a complete hold-and-spin round on a board of five columns and three rows. The board starts empty. There are no reels, paylines or bonus to trigger, so the round you pay for is the whole game. The theme is deep-sea salvage: a coin is a cargo crate, a respin is a breath of oxygen, and the clock counts the breaths you have left.

I have built three dives, Classic, Drift and Tank. They all return about 96% of the bet in the long run, and they differ in how long a round lasts and how much it swings. The maths is in [math.md](math.md) and the exact figures are in [par-sheet.md](par-sheet.md). The numbers in this document are written by `scripts/generate_docs.py` from the config and the reports.

## How a round plays

A round starts with an empty board and the dive's starting clock. On each spin every empty cell draws once. It lands a crate with a small chance or stays empty. A crate that lands stays in its cell until the round ends. After the spin the dive's clock rule runs, and that rule is the only thing that sets the dives apart. The round ends when the board is full or the clock reaches zero. If the board fills, any breaths left are lost.

The award is the sum of the coins on the board, plus the Grand if the board is full. It is paid once, at the end of the round. The bet is chosen before the round and stays fixed. The bets are 0.20, 0.40, 1.00, 2.00, 4.00, 10.00 credits.

Money inside the game is a whole number of units, where one unit is a thousandth of the bet. It becomes credits only at settlement, as units times the bet divided by 1,000, in decimal arithmetic. The smallest coin is 0.05x the bet, every value is a multiple of it, and every bet is a multiple of 0.20 credits, so a payout is always a whole number of cents.

## Coins, jackpots and the Grand

A crate holds one coin. The coin is drawn from a weight table, and each dive uses one table. There are eight cash coins and three jackpot coins. A jackpot coin is an ordinary crate with a bigger face. It takes one cell and pays its face, and nothing ever doubles or boosts it.

| Coin or prize | Value, in bets | Value, in units |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Cash crate | 0.05x | 50 |
| Cash crate | 0.1x | 100 |
| Cash crate | 0.2x | 200 |
| Cash crate | 0.25x | 250 |
| Cash crate | 0.5x | 500 |
| Cash crate | 1x | 1,000 |
| Cash crate | 2x | 2,000 |
| Cash crate | 3x | 3,000 |
| Mini jackpot | 5x | 5,000 |
| Minor jackpot | 20x | 20,000 |
| Major jackpot | 100x | 100,000 |
| Grand | 1,000x | 1,000,000 |

The Grand is not a coin. It is a prize of 1,000 bets that is paid on top of the board when all 15 cells are full. No award can pass 5,000 bets, and the largest award that can happen is 2,500 bets in Classic and Tank and 1,300 in Drift, so the cap never applies. The weight tables are in [par-sheet.md](par-sheet.md).

## The three dives

**Classic Dive.** The clock starts at 3 breaths. Whenever at least one crate lands, the clock goes back to 3. A spin that lands nothing costs one breath, so the round ends after 3 dead spins in a row. Each crate is a relief because it refills the air. A round pays nothing in 21.03% of cases.

**Drift Dive.** The round is exactly 6 spins, and nothing that lands changes the count. The only way a round is shorter is a full board. It is the calm dive, because it almost always pays something, with a hit frequency of 99.95%, and it has the lowest standard deviation of the three. Its weight table has no Major, which keeps the big coins out of it. The config calls this dive `Static`, and the lab accepts both `static` and `drift`.

**Tank Dive.** The clock starts at 4 breaths and nothing refills it, so every spin costs one. Air tanks land in empty cells like crates but hold no coin. A tank adds 1, 2 or 3 breaths and clears from its cell in the same spin. A round takes at most 3 tanks, and a tank drawn after the third counts as nothing. A round is short, about 5.01 spins, and a tank that lands on the last breath can save it.

|  | Classic Dive | Drift Dive | Tank Dive |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| RTP, exact | 96.0019% | 96.0004% | 96.0004% |
| Standard deviation of a round, in bets | 6.29 | 1.54 | 4.41 |
| Hit frequency | 78.97% | 99.95% | 99.86% |
| Mean spins | 7.40 | 6.00 | 5.01 |
| Mean crates on the final board | 3.13 | 6.01 | 5.74 |
| Grand, 1 in | 32,541 | 904,262 | 65,370 |
| Reachable maximum, in bets | 2,500 | 1,300 | 2,500 |
| RTP, simulated, 10,000,000 rounds, seed 1 | 96.2052% | 96.0002% | 96.1743% |

Standard deviation orders the dives as Drift, Tank and Classic, from lowest to highest. The client labels them Low, Low to medium and Medium in that order.

## The Grand

A full board needs all 15 cells filled, and a cell fills only when a crate happens to land on it. The Grand comes about 1 round in 32,541 in Classic, 1 in 65,370 in Tank and 1 in 904,262 in Drift. It adds only 3.2%, 1.6% and 0.1% of the RTP, so it is a small part of the return. It is a large part of the swing. The term it adds to $E[A^2]$ is 75.8% of the total in Classic and 75.1% in Tank, against 33.7% in Drift, which is why Classic and Tank swing so much even though most rounds are small.

## Design notes

Boards are sparse by design. Every bet buys a whole round, so the round itself has to return about 96% of the bet. The average coin is worth 0.2970, 0.1595 and 0.1645 of the bet in the three dives, far below one bet, and a final board holds on average only 3.13, 6.01 and 5.74 crates out of 15 cells. Busy boards would pay far more than the bet. A hold-and-spin feature that follows a base game can afford busy boards, because it is only part of the return. Here it is all of it, so the chance that a cell fills is small.

The one number I tuned is each dive's crate chance. It is frozen at the integer, out of 1,000,000, that puts the exact RTP closest to 96%, and a test checks that no neighbouring integer is closer. The ladder, the shapes of the weight tables, the Grand, the clock rules and the tank limit are design choices that I made and did not derive.

A round starts on an empty board, so a round can pay nothing. That happens in 21.03% of Classic rounds, 0.05% of Drift rounds and 0.14% of Tank rounds. I chose this over placing starting coins on the board, because those coins would need a draw of their own, and that draw would be a hidden base game.

The tank limit is a rule and also a convenience for the maths. Without it a tank that adds one breath can leave a state unchanged, and the exact solve would need a linear system on an unbounded state space. [math.md](math.md) explains this under Tank.

## The client

The client is a demo with play money. It is a Blazor WebAssembly app that runs the same engine as the lab, in the browser, so every round is played locally with no server and nothing is paid out. I draw the crates, medals, bottles, wells and the mark as SVG from a script in `scripts/art/`, in one flat style. The dark and the light theme share one palette for everything drawn on the board, because the board is deep water in both themes, and differ in the page and in the plates. The air tank is a toon render made in Blender from a script kept in `scripts/art/blender/`. It ships as two small WebP files, one for each theme, because a bitmap cannot follow the theme colours through CSS, and the page loads only the one that matches the theme. The water behind the page is drawn the same way: bands of deeper water, light shafts from above, a small school of fish, and on the seabed a wreck with a thread of air still rising from its bow, rocks and kelp. The art script keeps every tone of it dark or light enough for the page text to stay readable over it.

The page has two views of the same game. The player view is the default, and it shows the board, the clock, the board total, the balance, the bet and the result. A switch in the header, Show the maths, turns on the maths view, which adds what an analyst wants to read: the figures on the dive cards, the odds line on the result plate, and a side panel with the spins so far, the counts of the round, the session tally and the spin log. The page remembers the switch in the browser's storage and still works when storage is blocked. The Math panel, which the M key also opens, is there in both views.

A player picks a dive and a bet and presses Dive. Each card is drawn as a place on the seabed, a wreck for Classic, a current that carries the crates for Drift and a weed bed for Tank, and under it are the name of the dive, one short line and its volatility drawn as one to three waves. The bet is a row of chips beside the Dive button. In the maths view the card gives the rule in full with the hit frequency, the typical length and the RTP, and a strip of three steps explains the genre.

In a round the board is the one thing to look at. It is as large as the window allows, framed like a hatch with a steel rim, and the jackpots sit in a row under it. Every cell of the board is a quiet recess, a well, and a coin that lands drops into it and settles, with a ring on the water and a few bubbles, so the board never changes shape. A gilded crate or a jackpot also catches the light once as it lands. A tile shows only its value on a plate under the coin, and its label stays in its name and its tooltip, so the page says the same with or without the pictures. A console at the foot of the board holds the clock, the board total and Skip. The clock is drawn: three oxygen bottles in Classic, six segments in Drift, and in Tank a bottle for each breath of air with the spare tanks beside them. A spin stays on the board for as long as what it held deserves: 450 milliseconds when nothing landed, 800 when crates landed, 1,300 when a jackpot landed and 1,100 on the last breath. On the last breath the rim turns amber, a tab shows on its top edge, the last bottle breathes slowly and the rim beats twice and rests, like a heart, about once every one and a half seconds. Only the transform and the opacity of those change, so nothing on the page moves. The water keeps the clock as well. As the air runs down, the board and, on a large screen, the page behind it darken by a step, and a crate that refills the air opens the water again, so the last breath is the darkest moment and the crates are lit against it. When the round ends the dive surfaces and the water clears. A jackpot that lands gives one ring on its tile and one on its card, and the board total counts up for longer.

When a round ends, the console becomes the result plate, and the result rises into it as the water clears, with Dive again beside it and Change dive after it. The number is set in the sans face with lining figures. A round that returns less than the bet shows a muted number, a round that returns the bet or more shows it in amber, and a round of ten times the bet or more says Big win over the number, with the Major medal turning in beside it and an amber edge on the plate. On a big win the coins on the board light one after another, each once, while the number counts up from nothing, and a few bubbles rise through the water. A round that was skipped shows its number at once and keeps only the lights. A round that returns nothing says it surfaced with nothing.

The maths view puts the multiple of the bet under the number, or for a round under the bet how much of the bet came back, and a line on how likely a result at least that good is. A win is put as how many dives in some number do at least that well, a round under the bet as how many dives in ten return less than the bet, those that pay nothing included, and a round with nothing as how many dives surface with nothing. The figures come from the exact award distribution of the solver, which the page builds once for each dive, a few milliseconds of work, from the final crate probabilities in the report. The side panel lists what landed, newest first, with each run of spins that landed nothing as one row, and the Skip key plays out the rest of a round. When the round is over the list folds into a line, Spin by spin, which opens on request and takes the room of the history strip while it is open. The counts of the round leave jackpots out of the crates and count them on their own line. After the first round the panel keeps a tally of the session: the rounds played, the total bet, the total returned and a strip of the last twelve results, in which ten times the bet fills the height and a round that returns nothing is a thin tick. The legend names the three kinds of bar that carry a colour. The share returned so far appears from the tenth round, with the number of rounds it rests on, because a share of a few rounds says nothing. The page holds the tally in memory only and clears it with the balance. It sits next to the exact return of the dive from the reports, because a short session says little.

The page itself never scrolls. From a phone to a wide screen the selection and the round fit between the header and the footer, and only the maths view on a phone held upright scrolls the part between them, because its side panel sits under the board. The balance is play money and has a reset button. A reduce-motion setting turns off the drop and the splash of a new coin, the count-up of the board total, the flying numbers, the beat of the last breath, the rise of the result, the lights and the count of a big win, and the bubbles behind the page, and it applies by itself when the system asks for reduced motion. With reduced motion the steps of the water stay and only the fade goes, and the ring of a jackpot is still. Until the game has loaded, the page shows the mark, an empty board and one line, drawn in the page colours and not animated.

The dive cards of the maths view and the Math panel read their figures from the reports when the site is built, so they show the numbers in [par-sheet.md](par-sheet.md). The Math panel also shows the seed of the most recent round, and `lab play --dive <dive> --seed <seed>` replays that round in the console. Opening the site with `?seed=<number>` makes the rounds repeatable, which the browser tests use.

The browser tests run in Chromium by default, and setting `E2E_BROWSERS=all` runs them in Firefox and in WebKit, the engine behind Safari, where they pass as well. I have not tried the client on a real Mac or iPhone, and I have not tried it with a screen reader. Free, Wreck and Crew are not built, and nothing in this repository computes them.
